title: The scholar who said if
hookLine: Kumarila falls from a tower crying 'if the Vedas are true', and Mimamsa holds the Veda apaurusheya: heard, never written
carry: apaurusheya: the veda is heard, not written
tomorrow: the fire god runs off with the gods' treasure and weeps silver tears. why tell a story in a book of rules?

cards: A young scholar named Kumarila does something bold. To learn how Buddhist teachers argue against the Veda, he goes to study among them. One day, as his teacher criticizes the Veda, Kumarila weeps, and his secret is out.
In the telling, he falls, or is thrown, from the top of a tall tower. As he falls, he cries out: if the Vedas are true, I will live. He lands alive.
But he loses one eye. And later he says why. Because of one word.
If. For one moment, he had doubted.

teach.b: The story comes from a later life of Shankara. Kumarila Bhatta was real, one of Mimamsa's greatest thinkers. What would he risk a fall for?
The idea at the heart of today. All week, Mimamsa's method has rested on one thing: dharma is known through the Veda's words, and nothing else can see it. So the words had better be reliable.
If a person wrote them, a person could be wrong.
Jaimini's fifth sutra says the bond between a word and its meaning is original. Nobody invented it. So the Veda's instruction is a true means of knowing dharma, depending on nothing else.
Later Mimamsa thinkers, Kumarila among them, spell out the consequence: the Veda is apaurusheya, not made by any person. The rishis didn't compose it. They're called seers; they saw and heard it.
That's why the Veda is called shruti, what is heard. Jaimini even meets an objection: parts of the Veda carry people's names.
Those names, he answers, come from the ones who taught and recited those parts, not from authors. This is why Vedic chanting is guarded so fiercely.
Students still learn each hymn by ear from a teacher, in patterns that repeat the words one by one and in pairs, so not one syllable slips.
If no person made the words, no one's mistake is hiding in them, and no one edits them. Other Hindu schools see the Veda's origin differently, and the tradition keeps them all in the conversation.
For Kumarila, one doubting if cost an eye.

how: Vedic hymns are still learned by ear from a teacher, in recitation patterns that guard every syllable; Mimamsa holds that the Veda is apaurusheya, not authored by any person, which is why its injunctions can be trusted as the way to know dharma.

games.why: for Mimamsa the words have no author, so no human mistake hides in them, and they're kept syllable by syllable.

practice: Bring to mind one line you were given and have never changed: a mantra, a blessing, a verse, a prayer from home. Say it once, slowly, exactly as it was taught to you, every syllable.
If you pray, let that line be your prayer, and rest in the quiet after it. If you don't, notice what it feels like to say words you didn't write.
